Q17583803.summary: This rectangular marble pillar from the destroyed cloister of Narbonne Cathedral carries a figure on each of its four faces. The face shown here is a crowned, enthroned ruler holding a sceptre, whose identity the museum considers unknown; on another face the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child on her lap, holding a book, and two martyrs with palms occupy the remaining sides. Though enigmatic, the pillar is one of the finest survivals of Romanesque sculpture from Narbonne.
facts: The Musée des Augustins says the pillar probably comes from the former cloister of Saint-Just Cathedral, Narbonne, and that its date, iconography and purpose remain enigmatic.
The two martyrs may be Saints Justus and Pastor, the cathedral's patrons.
The monolithic marble pillar is 131 cm high and entered the museum by 1835.
Q17583803.notes: The image shows only the face with the crowned figure (catalogued as 'God the Father', though the museum's own commentary calls him a king of unknown identity); the Christ Child appears on another face that is not illustrated. A photograph of the Virgin-and-Child face would be preferable. The museum dates the pillar to the 12th century (1101–1200), not the 11th as Wikidata does.
Q17583803.original_title: Dieu, la Vierge à l'Enfant et deux martyrs

Q29226952.summary: At the centre of this richly carved leaf Christ hangs on a broad cross, his arms outstretched over two inscribed plaques, with a titulus above his head; around him crowd tiny scenes of the Passion and its aftermath, including the Virgin and John, soldiers with lance and sponge, a meal at a table at lower left and a domed tomb at right. Above, busts in medallions and further scenes complete the story. Framed by a border of fluted fans and pearls, it is one of the most ambitious Carolingian ivories of the Crucifixion.
facts: The French heritage database records the inscriptions HIC EST IHS NAZARENUS REX IUDEOR on the titulus and, on the arms of the cross, 'MULIER ECCE FILIUS TUUS' and 'APLE ECCE MATER TUA' (Woman, behold thy son; Apostle, behold thy mother).

Once classified as 12th-century, it was re-dated to the 9th century; a 1992 study by André Bonnery attributed it to Aachen at the end of Charlemagne's reign, and it was shown at the 2014 Charlemagne exhibition in Aachen.
The plaque measures 25.3 × 15.7 cm and probably served as a book cover; it has been a protected historic object since 1901.
Q29226952.notes: Individual small scenes are described cautiously from the photograph; their identification was not checked against a scholarly catalogue.
Q29226952.original_title: Croix glorieuse; Scènes de la vie du Christ

cur:monumental-kalenderhane-presentation.summary: This fragment preserves the Virgin, in a dark blue maphorion, holding out the haloed Christ Child towards the aged Simeon, whose head and hands appear at the right; the rest of the composition is lost. The figures are drawn with a delicate sensitivity in small, finely set tesserae.
facts: The roughly one-metre-square mosaic, found during the restoration of the Kalenderhane Mosque (the former church of the Theotokos Kyriotissa), is described as the only pre-Iconoclastic mosaic of a religious subject surviving in Istanbul.
The same building preserved 13th-century frescoes of the life of Saint Francis, the oldest known cycle of the saint.

cur:monumental-kalenderhane-presentation.notes: The photographer dates the fragment to the late 6th or early 7th century; captions on other Commons photographs of the same mosaic give 'probably about 12th century'. The pre-Iconoclast date is followed here, in agreement with Wikipedia.
